claim: Serotonin plays a critical role in regulating many behaviors that rely on olfaction.
source: Serotonin plays a critical role in regulating many behaviors that rely on olfaction and recently there has been great effort in determining how this molecule functions in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general background claim about serotonin's role in olfaction-dependent behaviors.

claim: It remains unknown how serotonergic neurons that innervate the first olfactory relay respond to odor stimulation.
source: However, it remains unknown how serotonergic neurons that innervate the first olfactory relay respond to odor stimulation and how they integrate synaptically into local circuits.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Nearly all odors inhibit the CSDn cells.
source: We report that nearly all odors inhibit these cells, likely through connections made reciprocally within the antennal lobe.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on experimental observations.

claim: The CSDn cells are inhibited through connections made reciprocally within the antennal lobe.
source: We report that nearly all odors inhibit these cells, likely through connections made reciprocally within the antennal lobe.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data about the mechanism of inhibition.

claim: The CSDn neurons likely release acetylcholine in addition to serotonin.
source: Pharmacological and immunohistochemical analyses reveal that these neurons likely release acetylcholine in addition to serotonin and that exogenous and endogenous serotonin have opposing effects on olfactory responses.
evidence: This is based on pharmacological and immunohistochemical experimental data.

claim: Exogenous and endogenous serotonin have opposing effects on olfactory responses.
source: Pharmacological and immunohistochemical analyses reveal that these neurons likely release acetylcholine in addition to serotonin and that exogenous and endogenous serotonin have opposing effects on olfactory responses.
evidence: This is a finding from experimental comparisons of exogenous and endogenous serotonin effects.

claim: Activation of the entire serotonergic network may be required for persistent serotonergic modulation of pheromone responses in the antennal lobe.
source: Finally, we show that activation of the entire serotonergic network, as opposed to only activation of those fibers innervating the antennal lobe, may be required for persistent serotonergic modulation of pheromone responses in the antennal lobe.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on optogenetic experiments comparing CSDn-specific versus whole network activation.

claim: Behaviors that rely critically on olfaction depend on proper serotonin signaling.
source: Behaviors that rely critically on olfaction also depend on proper serotonin signaling (Albin et al., 2015; Lent et al., 1989; Kravitz, 2000; Dierick and Greenspan, 2007; Becnel et al., 2011; Johnson et al., 2011; Ganesh et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Serotonergic neurons in both mammals and insects show stimulus evoked responses.
source: Serotonergic neurons in both mammals and insects show stimulus evoked responses (Ranade and Mainen, 2009; Hill et al., 2002; Cohen et al., 2015), but in no phylogenetic group have the odor responses been comprehensively mapped for serotonergic neurons that project to the first olfactory relay.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies in mammals and insects.

claim: In no phylogenetic group have the odor responses been comprehensively mapped for serotonergic neurons that project to the first olfactory relay.
source: Serotonergic neurons in both mammals and insects show stimulus evoked responses (Ranade and Mainen, 2009; Hill et al., 2002; Cohen et al., 2015), but in no phylogenetic group have the odor responses been comprehensively mapped for serotonergic neurons that project to the first olfactory relay.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge across phylogenetic groups.

claim: In mammals, serotonin indirectly inhibits olfactory receptor neurons in the olfactory bulb.
source: For example, in mammals serotonin indirectly inhibits olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) in the olfactory bulb (OB) (Petzold et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Only one pair of serotonergic interneurons (CSDns) project to the antennal lobes in Drosophila.
source: More importantly, as with several other insect species, only one pair of serotonergic interneurons termed the contralaterally-projecting serotonin-immunoreactive deuterocerebral interneurons (CSDns), project to the first olfactory relay, the antennal lobes (AL) (Kent et al., 1987; Sun et al., 1993; Dacks et al., 2006) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: The CSDns are directly involved in pheromone-mediated behaviors such as courtship.
source: In flies, mechanisms exist to label and manipulate this neuron (Singh et al., 2013; Roy et al., 2007), and recent studies have shown the CSDns to be directly involved in pheromone-mediated behaviors such as courtship (Singh et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The CSDns are predominantly inhibited by olfactory stimulation.
source: Our results demonstrate that these neurons, the CSDns, are predominantly inhibited by olfactory stimulation, and that this inhibition arises from reciprocal synapses formed directly within the AL.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on experimental data.

claim: The inhibition of CSDns arises from reciprocal synapses formed directly within the antennal lobe.
source: Our results demonstrate that these neurons, the CSDns, are predominantly inhibited by olfactory stimulation, and that this inhibition arises from reciprocal synapses formed directly within the AL.
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing reciprocal connectivity.

claim: The CSDn likely releases acetylcholine.
source: We show that the CSDn likely also releases the fast-acting neurotransmitter, acetylcholine (ACh), and that these two molecules produce different effects with opposing polarities and time courses on their downstream targets.
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemical and pharmacological data.

claim: Acetylcholine and serotonin from the CSDn produce different effects with opposing polarities and time courses on their downstream targets.
source: We show that the CSDn likely also releases the fast-acting neurotransmitter, acetylcholine (ACh), and that these two molecules produce different effects with opposing polarities and time courses on their downstream targets.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations of the effects of these neurotransmitters.

claim: Robust modulation of glomeruli that respond to cVA is only observed when the entire serotonergic network is stimulated in unison.
source: Finally, we report that despite the CSDns being the only serotonergic neurons to project to the AL, robust modulation of glomeruli that respond to the male pheromone, 11-cis-vaccenyl acetate (cVA), is only observed when the entire serotonergic network is stimulated in unison, rather than sole activation of the CSDns.
evidence: This is based on optogenetic experiments comparing different stimulation protocols.

claim: The CSDns are the only serotonergic neurons to project to the antennal lobe.
source: Finally, we report that despite the CSDns being the only serotonergic neurons to project to the AL, robust modulation of glomeruli that respond to the male pheromone, 11-cis-vaccenyl acetate (cVA), is only observed when the entire serotonergic network is stimulated in unison, rather than sole activation of the CSDns.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical studies cited earlier in the manuscript.

claim: Several odorants elicit rapid and diverse responses in CSDn cells.
source: Several odorants, such as ammonia and ethyl acetate, indeed elicited rapid and diverse responses in these cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Most olfactory stimuli suppress firing in the CSDn.
source: However, a broad panel of odorants spanning several chemical classes reveals that most olfactory stimuli actually suppress firing in the CSDn (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Esters are particularly effective at inhibiting the CSDn.
source: This sorting shows that esters, which are byproducts of fermentation, are particularly effective at inhibiting the CSDn (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The recruitment of inhibition within and between glomeruli in the antennal lobe does not largely depend on odor identity, but rather depends on total ORN activation.
source: The recruitment of inhibition within and between glomeruli in the antennal lobe does not largely depend on odor identity, but rather depends on total ORN activation (Hong and Wilson, 2015; Olsen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There is a strong correlation between antennal LFP amplitudes and the strength of inhibition onto the CSDn.
source: We measured such field potentials for a subset of our odor panel and found a strong correlation between antennal LFP amplitudes and the strength of inhibition onto the CSDn (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Two inhibitory neurotransmitters released by local interneurons have been identified in the antennal lobe: GABA and glutamate.
source: Two inhibitory neurotransmitters released by local interneurons (LNs) have been identified in the AL; GABA and glutamate (Liu and Wilson, 2013; Wilson and Laurent, 2005; Chou et al., 2010; Root et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Odor evoked inhibition of the CSDn is likely mediated in part by both GABA and glutamate transmitter systems.
source: Odor evoked inhibition of the CSDn is likely meditated in part by both transmitter systems, as bath application of their respective antagonists block this inhibition (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is based on pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: The CSDn expresses dSerT-eGFP in the antennal lobe, confirming that it releases 5-HT within this structure.
source: We expressed a serotonin reuptake transporter fused to eGFP (dSerT-eGFP) in the CSDns (Park et al., 2006). This molecule localized in the AL confirming that the CSDns release 5-HT within this structure.
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemical data showing dSerT-eGFP localization.

claim: The CSDn has postsynaptic sites in the antennal lobe.
source: To determine if the CSDns also have postsynaptic sites in the AL, we expressed the dendritic marker, DenMark (Nicolai et al., 2010). The positive labeling observed for both molecules suggests that the CSDn forms reciprocal connections within the antennal lobe (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemical data showing DenMark expression.

claim: The CSDn forms reciprocal connections within the antennal lobe.
source: The positive labeling observed for both molecules suggests that the CSDn forms reciprocal connections within the antennal lobe (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of both pre- and postsynaptic markers.

claim: Labeling for both dSerT-eGFP and DenMark was found throughout the antennal lobe suggesting that all glomeruli interact with the CSDn in a bidirectional manner to some extent.
source: Specifically, we found labeling for both markers throughout the AL suggesting that all glomeruli interact with the CSDn in a bidirectional manner to some extent.
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemical observations.

claim: The anterior lateral glomeruli, including DA1 and VA1d, had the least staining for both dSerT-eGFP and DenMark markers.
source: Notably, the anterior lateral glomeruli, including DA1 and VA1d, which both process pheromones, had the least staining for both markers.
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemical observations.

claim: The CSDn's dendrites within the antennal lobe show sensitivity to GABA, glutamate, and acetylcholine.
source: The CSDn's dendrites within the AL show sensitivity to GABA, glutamate, and acetylcholine (Figure 2H–J).
evidence: This is based on pressure injection experiments shown in Figure 2H-J.

claim: The CSDn is inhibited by odors proportional to the total number of ORNs activated, and this inhibition functionally arises from local connections within the antennal lobe.
source: Combined these data suggest that the CSDn is inhibited by odors proportional to the total number of ORNs activated, and that this inhibition functionally arises from local connections within the AL.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experimental findings.

claim: Stimulation of the CSDn results in a brief depolarization of local interneurons followed by a delayed hyperpolarization.
source: Stimulation of the CSDn results in a brief depolarization of the LNs followed by a delayed hyperpolarization.(Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on optogenetic stimulation experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The serotonin receptor antagonist methysergide is not effective at blocking the excitatory synapse from the CSDn to local interneurons.
source: Surprisingly, the potent 5-HT receptor antagonist, methysergide, is not effective at blocking this excitatory synapse (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is based on pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: The CSDn may release another neurotransmitter in addition to serotonin.
source: This result suggests that the CSDn may release another neurotransmitter in addition to serotonin.
evidence: This is inferred from the failure of methysergide to block the excitatory response.

claim: Methysergide blocked the delayed hyperpolarization in local interneurons caused by CSDn stimulation.
source: Methysergide (50 μM, red) bocked the delayed hyperpolarization but has no effect on the depolarization.
evidence: This is based on pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Mecamylamine blocked the depolarization in local interneurons caused by CSDn stimulation.
source: Mecamylamine (100 μM, blue) blocked the depolarization.
evidence: This is based on pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The CSDn is labeled by the ChAT-Gal4 promoter line.
source: Consistent with this notion, we found that the CSDn is labeled by the ChAT-Gal4 promoter line, and that it is immunopositive for both ChAT and VAchT (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The CSDn is immunopositive for both ChAT and VAchT.
source: Consistent with this notion, we found that the CSDn is labeled by the ChAT-Gal4 promoter line, and that it is immunopositive for both ChAT and VAchT (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Brief pulses of red light resulted in broad plateau potentials in CSDns expressing NaChBac and Chrimson.
source: Brief pulses of red light resulted in broad plateau potentials in CSDns expressing NaChBac and Chrimson (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: NaChBac plateau potentials were sufficient to elicit a brief depolarization and a strong hyperpolarization in local interneurons.
source: Such potentials were sufficient to elicit a brief depolarization and a strong hyperpolarization in LNs (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is based on TERPS experiments shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The hyperpolarization in local interneurons was blocked by methysergide, but neither methysergide nor mecamylamine blocked the depolarization.
source: The hyperpolarization was blocked by methysergide, but neither methysergide nor mecamylamine blocked the depolarization (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is based on TERPS experiments with pharmacology shown in Figure 3J.

claim: The depolarization in local interneurons is likely mediated by electrical coupling.
source: This depolarization is thus likely mediated by electrical coupling.
evidence: This is inferred from the insensitivity to both methysergide and mecamylamine.

claim: The serotonergic connections from the CSDn to the local interneurons are likely monosynaptic.
source: Together these data show that the serotonergic connections from the CSDn to the LNs are likely monosynaptic, while the acetylcholinergic connections appear polysynaptic.
evidence: This is based on TERPS experiments that isolate monosynaptic connections.

claim: The acetylcholinergic connections from the CSDn to the local interneurons appear polysynaptic.
source: Together these data show that the serotonergic connections from the CSDn to the LNs are likely monosynaptic, while the acetylcholinergic connections appear polysynaptic.
evidence: This is based on TERPS experiments and pharmacological analysis.

claim: The connections between the CSDn and projection neurons appear highly similar to those observed between the CSDn and local interneurons, only much smaller in amplitude.
source: We found that the connections appear highly similar to those observed between the CSDn and LNs, only much smaller in amplitude.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations comparing CSDn effects on PNs and LNs.

claim: CSDn stimulation resulted in a brief depolarization of projection neurons followed by a delayed hyperpolarization.
source: CSDn stimulation resulted in a brief depolarization of the PNs followed by a delayed hyperpolarization.
evidence: This is based on optogenetic stimulation experiments.

claim: Most of the excitatory connections from the CSDn onto projection neurons are polysynaptic.
source: TERPS analysis revealed that most of the excitatory connections onto the PNs are also polysynaptic while the serotonergic connections are likely direct.
evidence: This is based on TERPS experiments.

claim: The serotonergic connections from the CSDn onto projection neurons are likely direct.
source: TERPS analysis revealed that most of the excitatory connections onto the PNs are also polysynaptic while the serotonergic connections are likely direct.
evidence: This is based on TERPS experiments.

claim: Serotonin functions naturally to suppress DA1 responses.
source: This suggests that serotonin functions naturally to suppress DA1 responses and that methysergide removes this suppression.
evidence: This is inferred from the effect of methysergide on DA1 responses.

claim: Fluoxetine decreased DA1 projection neuron odor responses.
source: Consistent with an inhibitory function for serotonin, fluoxetine decreased DA1 PN odor responses (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 6D (note: this appears to be a typo in the manuscript, should be Figure 5D).

claim: In all three glomeruli tested (DA1, DM6, and DL5), odor responses diminished as serotonergic transmission increased.
source: In all three glomeruli that tested, we found that odor responses diminished as serotonergic transmission increased (Figure 5E–G).
evidence: This is based on pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 5E-G.

claim: Exogenous serotonin reliably enhanced odor responses.
source: We show that exogenous serotonin reliably enhanced odor responses despite the finding that manipulating endogenous transmission suppresses odor responses (Figure 5H–J).
evidence: This is based on experiments with exogenous serotonin application shown in Figure 5H-J.

claim: Chronic activation of the CSDn with a 10-Hz sine wave of red light did not significantly modulate DA1 responses to cVA.
source: This chronic activation of the CSDn did not significantly modulate DA1 responses to cVA (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is based on optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: Odor-evoked activity in the CSDn driven by ammonia failed to modulate DA1 odor responses.
source: This odor-evoked activity in the CSDn also failed to modulate DA1 odor responses.
evidence: This is based on experiments where ammonia was used to drive CSDn activity.

claim: Activation of the whole serotonergic system using the Trh-Gal4 promoter produced a long-lasting suppression of DA1 odor responses.
source: Activation of the whole serotonergic system produced a long-lasting suppression of odor responses.
evidence: This is based on optogenetic experiments using Trh-Gal4 to activate all serotonergic neurons.

claim: Serotonin from sources other than the CSDn may contribute to the modulation of DA1 odor responses.
source: Second, they suggest that 5-HT from sources other than the CSDn may contribute to the modulation of DA1 odor responses.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference between CSDn-specific and whole network stimulation effects.

claim: DA1 sensitivity to serotonergic pharmacology remains even when the CSDn is ablated.
source: Even in the absence of viable CSDns, the application of methysergide potentiated PN responses in the DA1 glomerulus (Figure 7E and F), suggesting that serotonergic neurons outside the AL contribute in modulating PN responses.
evidence: This is based on experiments with diphtheria toxin ablation of CSDns shown in Figure 7E and F.

claim: Serotonergic neurons outside the antennal lobe contribute to modulating projection neuron responses.
source: Even in the absence of viable CSDns, the application of methysergide potentiated PN responses in the DA1 glomerulus (Figure 7E and F), suggesting that serotonergic neurons outside the AL contribute in modulating PN responses.
evidence: This is inferred from the persistence of methysergide effects after CSDn ablation.

claim: When all 5-HT neurons are ablated using diphtheria toxin with the Trh promoter, no potentiation by methysergide is seen.
source: We also expressed diphtheria toxin in all 5-HT neurons using the Trh promoter (Figure 7G). In this case, no potentiation was seen suggesting the boosting by methysergide was not caused by off target effects (Figure 7H and I).
evidence: This is based on experiments with complete serotonergic system ablation shown in Figure 7G-I.

claim: Chronic Chrimson activation of the CSDn did not modulate VA1d projection neuron odor responses.
source: As with DA1, we saw no modulation of VA1d PN odor responses during chronic Chrimson activation of the CSDn (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: This is based on optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: Brief pulses of light to drive the CSDn transiently during the peak of VA1d odor responses revealed a small but significant increase in the VA1d responses during CSDn stimulation.
source: This protocol revealed a small but significant increase in the VA1d responses during CSDn stimulation.
evidence: This is based on optogenetic experiments with brief stimulation.

claim: CSDn activation added about 1 action potential per projection neuron per odor response in the VA1d glomerulus.
source: In total, CSDn activation added about 1 action potential per PN per odor response in this glomerulus.
evidence: This is based on quantification of optogenetic experiments.

claim: The small boost in VA1d firing during CSDn stimulation is more likely to be caused by acetylcholine from the CSDn rather than serotonin.
source: Because CSDn stimulation boosted rather than suppressed VA1d responses, it is more likely to be caused by acetylcholine from the CSDn rather than serotonin.
evidence: This is inferred from the direction of the effect and the known actions of these neurotransmitters.

claim: The small boost in VA1d firing was observed in the presence of methysergide, further suggesting it is not mediated by 5-HT.
source: Indeed, this small boost in VA1d firing was observed in the presence of methysergide, further suggesting it is not mediated by 5-HT (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is based on pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Brief stimulation of the CSDn did not modulate DA1 glomerulus responses.
source: We repeated this brief stimulation protocol on the DA1 glomerulus, where we found no evidence of modulation (Figure 8, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The CSDn may not contribute heavily to the modulation of pheromones in flies.
source: These results suggest that the CSDn may not contribute heavily to the modulation of pheromones in flies.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of strong modulation in pheromone-sensitive glomeruli.

claim: The predominant role of serotonin in the Drosophila antennal lobe is to suppress projection neuron odor responses.
source: We found that the predominant role of serotonin in the Drosophila AL is to suppress PN odor responses and this effect is seen across PNs that innervate different glomeruli.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experimental findings.

claim: Serotonin suppression is observed in glomeruli both sensitive to pheromones and food-derived odors.
source: We observed suppression in glomeruli both sensitive to pheromones and food-derived odors, suggesting a common theme across olfactory channels.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations across different glomeruli.

claim: Previous studies in moths and Drosophila have suggested the opposite role for serotonin in modulating insect olfaction.
source: Interestingly, previous studies in moths and Drosophila have suggested the opposite role for serotonin in modulating insect olfaction (Dacks et al., 2009; Kloppenburg et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In previous studies, the application of exogenous serotonin results in the boosting of olfactory responses in projection neurons.
source: In these studies, the application of exogenous serotonin results in the boosting of olfactory responses in PNs.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from previous studies.

claim: The difference between exogenous and endogenous serotonin effects is attributed to the mode of application.
source: We attribute this difference to the mode of application, namely exogenous versus endogenous release.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of the discrepancy.

claim: Multiple classes of 5-HT receptors within the antennal lobe each have unique kinetics, affinities, and ability to excite or inhibit neurons.
source: An alternative explanation might be that multiple classes of 5-HT receptors within the antennal lobe each have unique kinetics, affinities, and ability to excite or inhibit neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed differences.

claim: 5-HT7 and 5-HT1B receptors are both found in the antennal lobe of the fly.
source: For example, 5-HT7 (Becnel et al., 2011) and 5-HT1B (Yuan et al., 2005; Singh et al., 2013) receptors are both found in the AL of the fly, but the 5-HT7 receptor is fully saturated before the 5-HT1B receptor begins to show any sensitivity to 5-HT (Gasque et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Transient release of serotonin from the CSDn elicited only a brief excitatory inward current in local interneurons and projection neurons and a more prolonged outward inhibitory current.
source: For example, we found that transient release of serotonin from the CSDn elicited only a brief excitatory inward current in LNs and PNs and a more prolonged outward inhibitory current (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Bath application of 5-HT resulted in a prolonged inward current that lasted the duration of 5-HT exposure.
source: However, bath application of 5-HT resulted in a prolonged inward current that lasted the duration of 5-HT exposure (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In crayfish, the rate of bath application of serotonin determines whether it will facilitate or depress synaptic input onto command neurons that trigger escape behaviors.
source: In crayfish, the rate of bath application of serotonin determines whether it will facilitate or depress synaptic input onto command neurons that trigger escape behaviors (Teshiba et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: DA1 is highly sensitive to serotonergic pharmacology, yet largely insensitive to serotonin from the CSDn.
source: Interestingly, we found that DA1 is highly sensitive to serotonergic pharmacology, yet largely insensitive to serotonin from the CSDn.
evidence: This is based on experimental comparisons of pharmacological and optogenetic approaches.

claim: DA1 sensitivity to serotonergic pharmacology remains even when the CSDn is ablated.
source: In fact, DA1 sensitivity to serotonergic pharmacology remains even when the CSDn is ablated.
evidence: This is based on experiments with CSDn ablation.

claim: The DA1 glomerulus is only weakly innervated by the CSDn.
source: This lack of DA1 sensitivity to CSDn-derived serotonin is consistent with the finding that this glomerulus is only weakly innervated by the CSDn (Singh et al., 2013), but is still surprising given that the CSDn is the only serotonergic neuron that innervates the AL (Kent et al., 1987; Sun et al., 1993; Dacks et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Serotonin released from Trh-Gal4 stimulation may modulate cells outside the antennal lobe that are inaccessible to the CSDn and that ultimately feedback into the antennal lobe.
source: First, serotonin released from Trh-Gal4 stimulation may modulate cells outside the AL that are inaccessible to the CSDn and that ultimately feedback into the AL.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism to explain the experimental observations.

claim: Stimulation of Trh-Gal4 may elevate serotonin in the antennal lobe through paracrine signaling to levels higher than can be achieved by the CSDn alone.
source: Second, stimulation of Trh-Gal4 may elevate serotonin in the AL through paracrine signaling to levels higher than can be achieved by the CSDn alone.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism to explain the experimental observations.

claim: Serotonin can be readily measured in the haemolymph of many invertebrates.
source: This paracrine or hormonal function for serotonin may not be so surprising considering serotonin can be readily measured in the haemolymph of many invertebrates (Panksepp et al., 2003; Tecott, 2007; Lange et al., 1989), and neuronal activity alone is sufficient to raise circulating 5-HT in invertebrate models (Levenson et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In fly larvae, a single 30 s bout of activity in serotonergic neurons can drastically elevate 5-HT levels for several minutes as measured extracellularly by fast-scan cyclic voltammetry.
source: In the fly larvae, a single 30 s bout of activity in serotonergic neurons can drastically elevate 5-HT levels for several minutes as measured extracellularly by fast-scan cyclic voltammetry (Borue et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Earlier studies proposed a polarity in the CSDn's neurites and suggested that it integrates input from higher protocerebral circuits to modulate the antennal lobe in a top-down manner.
source: Earlier studies proposed a polarity in the CSDn's neurites and suggested that it integrates input from higher protocerebral circuits to modulate the AL in a top-down manner (Dacks et al., 2009; Hill et al., 2002; Sun et al., 1993; Roy et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The data is more consistent with a recent suggestion that the CSDn forms local circuits operating at the level of each glomerulus.
source: Our data is more consistent with a recent suggestion that the CSDn forms local circuits operating at the level of each glomerulus (Kloppenburg and Mercer, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study and the authors' experimental findings.

claim: Both pre- and postsynaptic specializations were found throughout virtually all glomeruli in the antennal lobe.
source: We found both pre- and postsynaptic specializations throughout virtually all glomeruli in the AL and confirmed that these connections are functional.
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemical and physiological data.

claim: Cellular correlates of both synaptic inputs and outputs are present in CSDn arbors within the lateral horn.
source: Additionally, we show cellular correlates of both synaptic inputs and outputs in CSDn arbors within the LH (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemical data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Top-down modulation is not the exclusive function of the CSDn.
source: Together this anatomical and physiological evidence argues at minimum that top-down modulation is not the exclusive function of the CSDn.
evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical and physiological evidence.

claim: Within the antennal lobe, the CSDn makes connections onto GABAergic local interneurons and most projection neurons.
source: Within the AL, we found that the CSDn makes connections onto GABAergic LNs and most PNs.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations of CSDn connectivity.

claim: Both local interneurons and projection neurons are inhibited by serotonin from the CSDn and are indirectly excited by acetylcholine during CSDn stimulation.
source: Both LNs and PNs are inhibited by serotonin from the CSDn and are indirectly excited by Ach during CSDn stimulation.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations of the effects of CSDn stimulation.

claim: The identity of the neurons that are monosynaptically connected to the CSDn via acetylcholine remains unknown.
source: However, the identity of the neurons that are monosynaptically connected to the CSDn via Ach remains unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current limitation of knowledge.

claim: CSDn stimulation alone was not sufficient to induce strong, lasting modulation in pheromone sensitive glomeruli.
source: As mentioned above, CSDn stimulation alone was not sufficient to induce strong, lasting modulation in pheromone sensitive glomeruli.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: The CSDn might make odor responses more reliable across those glomeruli that it densely innervates.
source: An alternative hypothesis is that the CSDn might make odor responses more reliable across those glomeruli that it densely innervates.
evidence: This is a proposed hypothesis to explain the function of the CSDn.

claim: CSDn-evoked activity in projection neurons and local interneurons are virtually indistinguishable.
source: Functionally, the CSDn hyperpolarizes AL neurons through 5-HT and excites them in an Ach dependent manner. Interestingly, CSDn-evoked activity in PNs and LNs are virtually indistinguishable.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: The effect of CSDn stimulation became pronounced when local interneurons were depolarized by current injection and firing in local interneurons was suppressed via strong serotonergic inhibition.
source: Importantly though, the effect of CSDn stimulation became pronounced when LNs were depolarized by current injection and firing in LNs was suppressed via strong serotonergic inhibition (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3.

claim: CSDn spiking should serve to narrow the range of local interneuron and projection neuron activity, reduce membrane fluctuations arising from noise, and promote all odor responses to be initiated from a similar baseline.
